readerTitle: Two cleaners raised prices 40%. Only one got away with it.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가사 청소 서비스, 동네 철물점) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 프리미엄 가격은 가격표가 아니라 약속이다. 고객이 사기 전에 보고, 산 뒤에 확인할 수 있는 차이가 있어야 높은 가격이 유지된다.
misconception: 가격을 올리고 고급스럽게 포장하면 고객이 더 좋은 제품으로 여긴다.

sources.text: 마케팅·가격 전략의 표준 개념 (프리미엄 가격, 차별화)

factChecks.note: 청소 서비스 계산: 기존 $120 − 방문당 비용 $70 = $50. 프리미엄 $170 − ($70 + 추가 비용 $15) = $85. 기존 100회 × $50 = $5,000. 같은 이익에 필요한 방문 수 5,000 ÷ 85 = 58.8회(약 59회). 즉 방문의 약 41%를 잃어도 이익이 같습니다.
가격 인상률: $120 → $170은 41.7% 인상이며 카드에서는 "about 40%"로 표기했습니다. 두 회사의 고객 이탈 결과는 설명용 가상 시나리오입니다.

cards.title: Two cleaners raised prices 40%. Only one got away with it.
body: Two house-cleaning companies in the same town both moved from $120 to $170 a visit.
Within six months, one had lost a third of its clients. The other had a waiting list. The price was the same. What was behind it was not.

image.label: Two cleaning vans, one with a long queue of homes
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 같은 동네에 청소 서비스 밴 두 대. 한쪽 밴 앞에는 집 아이콘이 길게 줄 서 있고, 다른 쪽 밴에서는 집 아이콘들이 멀어진다. 두 밴에 똑같이 "$170" 가격표. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: You want to be the premium cleaner.
body: You run a house-cleaning service. You charge $120 a visit, about the same as everyone nearby. You want to move to $170 and be known as the high-end choice.

options.text: Rebrand as "luxury home care" with a new logo, uniforms and the new price
options.feedback: It looks premium on day one. But if the clean itself is the same, customers notice they are paying $50 more for the same result.

options.text: Add differences clients can see and check, like the same cleaner every visit and a free re-clean guarantee, then raise the price
options.feedback: It costs more to deliver, but it gives customers a reason to pay that they can test themselves. That's what holds a premium price up.

options.text: Charge $170 to new clients only and watch what happens
options.feedback: A safe test of demand. But it tests the price, not the reason to pay it, so you may learn little about what makes premium work.

cards.title: Same price. Different promise.
body: The first company changed its name, its vans and its price. The cleaning stayed the same. Regular clients compared notes, saw no difference, and many switched back to cheaper rivals.

The second company kept its name. It assigned one cleaner per home, left a signed checklist after each visit, and promised a free re-clean within 24 hours if anything was missed. That added about $15 a visit in cost. Then it raised the price.

cards.title: Why the second cleaner could afford to lose clients.
body: Before, 100 visits left $5,000. At the new price, about **59 visits** leave the same. The company could lose 4 in 10 visits and still earn as much.

cards.title: Premium pricing
body: **Premium pricing** means deliberately charging more than similar offers, and backing that price with a difference customers value.

The higher price is not the strategy. It's a promise. Customers accept it only when they can see the difference before buying and confirm it after. Without that, a premium price just looks like a worse deal.

image.label: A price tag resting on three pillars
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 큰 가격표 "$170"이 세 개의 기둥 위에 올려져 있다. 기둥 라벨: "Visible difference", "Proof", "Consistency". 기둥 하나가 빠진 버전이 옆에서 기울어지는 모습.

cards.title: What holds a premium price up.
body: Premium prices that last tend to rest on three things:
list: **A visible difference:** something customers notice, not just something you know
**Proof:** guarantees, reviews or checklists that let customers check the claim
**Consistency:** every visit, package and phone call matches the price
cards.callout: Remove one, and customers start comparing on price again.
cards.softwareNote: A premium software plan holds up when the extra is felt in daily use, like faster support, uptime promises or a named account contact. A higher price on the same features with a new plan name tends to raise churn, not revenue.

cards.title: Premium raises the bar on everything.
body: A higher price shrinks your market. Fewer people will buy, so the extra margin has to cover the lost volume.
Expectations rise too. A missed corner is a shrug at $120 and a complaint at $170. And rivals can copy visible extras, so the difference needs regular renewal.
Discounting is harder. Frequent sales tell customers the premium was never real.

cards.title: Now it's a local hardware store.
body: Your store sells the same branded power drills as a big chain ten minutes away. Customers can check the chain's price on their phones in seconds.
You want higher margins. Where do you charge a premium?

options.text: Price everything 15% above the chain and count on local loyalty
options.feedback: Loyalty helps, but identical products are easy to compare. You'd be asking customers to pay more for nothing they can see.

options.text: Match the chain on identical items, and charge more where you add something, like setup help, sharpening or project kits
options.feedback: You avoid a losing price fight on identical goods and earn the premium where the difference is real and visible.

options.text: Cut prices to match the chain everywhere and win on friendly advice
options.feedback: You keep customers, but you give your real difference away for free. Good advice is often exactly what a premium can be charged for.

cards.title: A premium price is a promise customers can check.
body: Raise the price only after you've built a difference people can see, prove and get every time.
**Try it today:** write down why a customer should pay more for what you sell. Then ask: could they notice that before buying, and confirm it after?
